recension.note: The Russian recension — how the letters are named and read in the Slavonic sung in Moscow and Kyiv now. This is one living reading, not the only one: the Serbian and Bulgarian recensions differ, and no voice for either is installed on this machine. Milena reads Cyrillic as RUSSIAN, which is right for the consonants and wrong for the vowels: the recension's own rule is оканье, unstressed о read as [o] and never as [a], and that rule cannot be imposed on her — seven names say so.

0.why: The hard sign is silent in the recension and Milena treats it so: `say -v Milena "азъ"` is byte-identical to "аз" (e30f3187), which is exactly the church reading [as]. The а is stressed, so no reduction touches it, and Russian final devoicing of з to [s] is also what a lector does. This is the cleanest entry in the hall — one stressed open [a] and a voiceless sibilant, both correct.
0.compromise: Nothing material is lost. The one thing to note is that the ъ here is doing no work at all, which is the point: by the fourteenth century it was a mute orthographic sign, and the audio is evidence of that rather than of anything the tenth century said. To hear the letter's name with the jer still sounding, use the reconstruction.

1.why: Written with ы rather than и so that the second vowel is [ɨ], the recension's reading of ꙑ, and so the audio matches the hall's headword букꙑ rather than the later school spelling. The initial [b] is a true voiced stop — the whole reason this letter exists, since Greek beta had already gone to [v] and could not serve. Stress falls on бу, and Russian unstressed ы stays [ɨ] with only slight centralisation, so the word survives Milena's reduction almost intact. Parses as a word, 0.663 s at default rate, distinct from "буки" (0.673 s).
1.compromise: The living Russian church name is бу́ки with plain и, [ˈbukʲi], and that is what a Russian churchman actually says; this recipe follows the hall's older headword instead. The final vowel is very slightly laxer than a stressed [ɨ] would be.

2.why: Two problems solved by one substitution. Milena deletes ѣ outright, so it must be respelled — and е is precisely what the recension reads ѣ as, so the respelling is the tradition's own reading rather than a workaround. And "веди" is a real Russian word (the imperative of вести), so it comes from the lexicon with its stress known and fixed on the first syllable, where guesswork on a nonce string would be a coin-flip. The [v] is a clean labiodental fricative, the [dʲ] palatalised before the front vowel as Slavonic requires.
2.compromise: This is the later Russian name вѣ́ди, not the older вѣ́дѣ the hall gives as its headword — the hall's own note says both circulate and that the Russian tradition uses this one, so the living track is the right place for it. The final vowel reduces to [ɪ] where the recension would say a full [i]. Milena's е-spelling was checked against the ё-trap: "веди" and "вёди" are different files (0709171b against efcf6712), so there is no risk of [ˈvʲɵdʲɪ] here. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

3.why: The synodal norm reads г as a plosive [ɡ], and that is what Milena gives — the letter's own value, delivered twice. The stress falls on the second го, which is where глаго́ли carries it, and that syllable's о is therefore stressed and comes out as a full [o]: this is one of the few о-names akanye leaves alone, because the о is under the accent. Parses as a word, 0.828 s.
3.compromise: Two small losses in unstressed syllables. The first а is reduced to [ɐ] and the final и to [ɪ], where an unhurried lector gives [a] and [i]. Neither touches the letter's own sound. Worth telling the reader that the older Moscow and Old Believer usage, and the Ukrainian recension, read г as a fricative [ɣ] or [ɦ] in at least some words — this clip gives the synodal plosive, which is the commoner reading today but not the only one.

4.why: A real Russian word, so the stress is lexical and lands on the final syllable exactly as добро́ requires, and that final о is therefore full and unreduced [o]. The initial [d] is a true voiced dental stop and the r a Russian trill — both correct.
4.compromise: THIS IS THE AKANYE FAILURE, and it is the flagship of the problem, so it is stated plainly. Church Slavonic reading forbids Russian vowel reduction: a lector says [doˈbro], with the first о as clear as the second. Milena says [dɐˈbro], reducing the pretonic о towards [a]. It cannot be corrected. The combining acute is stripped before letter-to-sound — "добро", "добро́" and "до́бро" are one and the same file (c187e360, 0.708 s) — so there is no diacritic, no respelling and no rate that restores it. The alternative was Zosia's Polish "dobro", a real Polish word giving a genuinely unreduced [ˈdɔbrɔ]; it was rejected because it moves the stress to the wrong syllable, opens both vowels to [ɔ], and swaps a Russian voice for a Polish one in the middle of a Russian-recension track. Reduction against stress: the stress was judged the more audible error. To hear the word with both vowels clean, click through to the reconstruction, where it is Zosia's.

5.why: Word-initial е is [je] in Russian and in the recension alike, so the name announces the iotation that the separate letter ѥ exists to write. The vowel is stressed and therefore unreduced, and the hard sign is mute, giving a clean monosyllable [jest]. Checked against the ё-trap: "естъ" and "ёстъ" are different files (d619e8d8 against 87738c0b), so there is no risk of [jost].
5.compromise: The final т is devoiced and the ъ contributes nothing — correct for the recension, but it means the audio cannot distinguish ѥстъ from ѥсть, a distinction the manuscripts do make. Printed Church Slavonic writes есть with a soft sign and would give [jestʲ]; the hall's headword is hard, and this follows it.

6.why: The letter's own sound is the initial sibilant and it is correct: Russian ж is [ʐ], voiced, and the following и is automatically retracted to [ɨ] after it, which is what Slavonic жи does too. The spelling is живэте and not живете for a reason given in full below.
6.compromise: A trap and a trade. `say -v Milena "живете"` is BYTE-IDENTICAL to "живёте" (67d9867c, 0.808 s): Milena holds one lexical entry for that string, and the only Russian word spelt so is the verb живёте, with a stressed [ɵ]. Left alone this letter would have been announced 'zhiv-YO-tye', which is not the name of anything. Writing э forces the stressed vowel to [ɛ], which is right, at the price of de-palatalising the в: you hear [ʐɨˈvɛtʲɪ] where a lector says [ʐɨˈvʲete], with a soft [vʲ]. A hard consonant inside an unstressed-adjacent syllable was judged a much smaller error than the wrong stressed vowel in the letter's name. The final е still reduces to [ɪ]. Russian ж is also retroflex where the Slavonic sound was postalveolar — audible, but the same is true of every Russian reading of this letter.

7.why: Both archaic letters in this name are deleted by Milena — ѕ and ѣ each vanish without trace — so both are respelled, and both respellings are the recension's own reading: the Russian recension long ago lost the affricate and reads ѕ as a plain [z], and reads ѣ as [e]. So зело is not an approximation of the church reading, it is the church reading. The initial [zʲ] is palatalised before the front vowel, correctly.
7.compromise: Two things, and one of them is unverifiable. (1) The letter's own sound is GONE. Ѕ was made for the affricate [dz]; the Russian recension does not have it, so the audio gives [z] and the name no longer contains the sound it names. That is a fact about the living tradition, not a defect of the recipe — but it means anyone who wants to hear what this letter is for must use the reconstruction, where Polish supplies a true [dz]. (2) Stress is a real risk here that I cannot resolve without hearing it. Russian зело́ is an adverb stressed on the final syllable; the letter name is ѕѣ́ло, stressed on the first. If Milena takes the adverb's stress the word arrives as [zʲɪˈlo], which is the wrong shape entirely, and duration testing cannot tell the two apart (0.644 s either way). If she takes the first syllable, the final о then reduces to [ə] where the recension says [o]. Marked low because one of those two outcomes is certainly happening and I cannot say which.

8.why: A real Russian word, unchanged from the Slavonic in both spelling and meaning, so the stress is lexical and falls on the final syllable exactly where землꙗ́ carries it. The initial [zʲ] is the letter's own value, and the palatal [lʲ] before я is the same palatal lateral the manuscripts write. The final vowel is stressed and therefore full [a].
8.compromise: The pretonic е reduces to [ɪ] — ikanye, the front-vowel counterpart of akanye, and equally against church practice, which reads [zemˈlʲa]. Like akanye it cannot be steered out. This is a small error in a syllable that is not the letter, and everything the letter itself is about arrives correctly.

9.why: И́же is a real Russian word — the relative pronoun, still current in fixed phrases — so it comes from the lexicon with first-syllable stress secured, and the stressed vowel is therefore a clean full [i], which is the letter's whole content. Parses at 0.634 s.
9.compromise: The unstressed е after ж comes out as [ɨ] rather than [e], because Russian retracts unstressed vowels after the hard hushing consonants; a lector would say [ˈiʒe]. Nothing in the letter's own value is affected. This letter and the next are homophonous in the recension, as they have been since long before the recension existed — the distinction between them is graphic and numerical, never audible.

10.why: The letter names itself, and its name is a real Russian word, the conjunction 'and', which is also what the letter means. Read as a clean stressed [i] at 0.649 s — no reduction, since it carries the whole utterance. The rate is lowered to 140 as for every other monosyllable in this hall so the vowel is not clipped. Note that the letter itself, і at U+0456, CANNOT be used in the text: Milena deletes it — "іже" is 0.469 s against 0.634 s for "иже", and "большій" is byte-identical to "большй" (75e3cc24), proving the character is dropped, not read.
10.compromise: Audibly identical to и́же's first syllable and to the letter at index 9, which is correct — the two i-letters have never differed in sound, only in shape, in numeral value (10 against 8) and in scribal fashion. The living tradition often names this letter и десятеричное, 'i worth ten', precisely because the sound alone cannot distinguish them; that fuller name is not used here because the hall's label is the bare letter.

11.why: This letter has no place in the Russian recension at all — it never entered the Russian books, and Milena deletes the character outright (zero-length file). So there is nothing for a Russian voice to say. What survives is the Serbian usage, where the same letter is ђ and its value is [d͡ʑ], and Polish is the only voice installed that produces that affricate: Polish 'dzi' before a vowel is exactly [d͡ʑ]. 'Dzierwi' gives [ˈdʑɛrvʲi] — the affricate, a trilled r, and a final [i] standing for the front jer. Parses at 0.778 s.
11.compromise: The voice changes to Polish and the tradition changes with it: what you hear is a Serbian-recension value in a Polish mouth, offered because the Russian recension has no reading of this letter to give. Two mechanical losses. Polish devoices word-final obstruents, so the bare form 'dzierw' would end in [f]; the final i avoids that but converts the jer into a full vowel the letter name did not have. And the hall's own gloss allows [ɟ] as well as [dʑ] — a plain palatal stop, which Polish does not have and which nothing here can produce. Marked medium because the recipe is sound but the whole entry is a substitution for a reading that does not exist.

12.why: Russian and Slavonic [k] are both unaspirated, so the letter's own value is right twice over with no work at all — and it is worth saying that an English voice would have aspirated both stops and been wrong. The stress falls on the first syllable, as ка́ко requires, and that а is therefore full.
12.compromise: Akanye again, in its post-tonic form: the final о is reduced to [ə], so the word ends in a schwa where a lector says a clean [o] — [ˈkako]. This is the same failure as at Добро and is equally uncorrectable; see index 4 for the hash evidence. The word is otherwise exact.

13.why: The initial [lʲ] is the palatal variant the hall notes as л҄, delivered natively by Russian ль before ю, and it is the more interesting of the letter's two values. The word is spelt in full as людие rather than as the living люди so that the audio matches the hall's headword лю́диѥ. Parses as one word at 0.818 s.
13.compromise: Two caveats. The living Russian church name is лю́ди, two syllables, and that is what a churchman says; this is the older four-vowel form. And because людие is not a modern Russian word, its stress is Milena's guess rather than a lexical fact — the analogy with лю́ди makes first-syllable stress likely but not certain, and duration cannot test it. The medial и reduces to [ɪ]. The letter's plain [l], as against this palatal one, is not heard anywhere in the name.

14.why: A real Russian verb form, мы́слите, so the stress is lexical and falls on the first syllable exactly as мꙑ́слите requires — and that first syllable carries a genuine stressed [ɨ], the sound of ꙑ, which is a bonus the name was not chosen for. The [m] is a plain bilabial nasal, identical in both languages. Parses at 0.898 s.
14.compromise: Both unstressed front vowels reduce to [ɪ], so the word ends [-lʲɪtʲɪ] where the recension reads [-lite]. The living Russian church name is usually мысле́те, with a different vowel and a different stress; this follows the hall's headword instead. Nothing touches the letter's own sound.

15.why: The [n] is stressed-adjacent and initial, the vowel carries the stress and is a full [a], and the soft sign after ш is inert in Russian exactly as it is in the recension, since ш cannot be palatalised. So [naʂ] — a clean monosyllable and the letter's value delivered first.
15.compromise: The Slavonic name is на́шь with a genuinely soft [ʃʲ]; Russian ш is hard and retroflex, so the softness the ь writes is simply absent, and the audio cannot distinguish нашь from нашъ. Also, like Людиѥ, this letter has a palatal variant н҄ that the name does not contain — you hear the plain [n] only.

16.why: The one о-name akanye cannot touch, because the vowel is stressed and alone: [on], a full unreduced back vowel, with the mute hard sign contributing nothing. 'Он' is a real Russian word — the same pronoun, unchanged — so this comes from the lexicon. Of the seven names in this hall built on о, this is the only one that arrives exactly right, which makes it the reference point for hearing what the other six should have sounded like.
16.compromise: Russian stressed /o/ is close-mid [o] where the hall glosses the letter as open [ɔ]; the difference is small and is in any case a matter of which recension you are listening to. The hall's broad or round variant Ѻ ѻ is not a separate sound and has no separate recipe — Milena deletes that character too.

17.why: Russian initial [p] is unaspirated, as Slavonic [p] was, so the letter's value is right without intervention — an English voice would have aspirated it. 'Покои' is a real Russian word, so the stress is lexical and lands on the second syllable where поко́и carries it, making that о a full [o].
17.compromise: Akanye, in the pretonic position where it bites hardest: the first о is reduced towards [a], so you hear [pɐˈkoi] where a lector says [poˈkoj]. Uncorrectable — see index 4. There is a second, smaller point: покои is here three syllables with a final vowel [i], whereas the living name покой ends in a glide [j]; both spellings are current for the letter and the hall's headword has the vowel.

18.why: This is the living name exactly as printed Church Slavonic writes it, with the jer long since dropped and the vowel written ы. Russian delivers all three of the things it needs: a true alveolar trill for р, a plain [ts] affricate for ц, and [ɨ] for ы. Verified as a normally-read token, 0.644 s at default rate — worth stating because the Czech and Slovak voices both choke on the corresponding word (see the reconstruction's entry).
18.compromise: The Slavonic headword is рьци, with a front jer between р and ц and a plain [i] at the end; the recension has lost the jer and backed the vowel, so what you hear is [rtsɨ] where the tenth century said [rĭtsi]. That is a real historical change and not a defect, but it does mean the living name and the hall's transliteration will not obviously match. Whether the trill surfaces as a full multi-contact trill or a single tap is not something duration can establish.

19.why: A real Russian word, identical to the Slavonic in form and sense, so the stress is lexical and first-syllable as сло́во requires. The initial [s] is voiceless — Russian does not voice s before l — and the stressed о is full.
19.compromise: Akanye in its post-tonic form: the final о is a schwa [ə], where the recension reads [ˈslovo] with two clean back vowels. For the word that renders logos at the opening of John this is the most conspicuous place in the hall where the church rule and the Russian voice disagree, and it cannot be fixed — "слово" and "сло́во" are one file (6b14d1cb, 0.753 s). The reconstruction gives Zosia's Polish 'slowo' with both vowels intact, and clicking the two in succession is the clearest demonstration of what оканье means.

20.why: The recension resolves the Slavonic syllabic r of тврьдо into -вер-, giving тве́рдо, and that is the form used here. Russian [t] is unaspirated, as Slavonic [t] was. The spelling uses э rather than е for the reason below.
20.compromise: The second ё-trap, and it had to be routed around: `say -v Milena "твердо"` is BYTE-IDENTICAL to "твёрдо" (ddc6bb3a, 0.773 s), so Milena reads it as the ordinary Russian adverb with a stressed [ɵ] and the letter would have been announced 'TVYO-rdo'. Writing э forces [ɛ], which is the right vowel, and costs the palatalisation of the в — you hear [ˈtvɛrdə] where a lector says [ˈtvʲerdo]. Two further losses: the final о reduces to [ə], akanye again; and the syllabic r of the older тврьдо is not here at all, having been replaced by a full vowel. The reconstruction restores it, using a Czech word that still has the syllabic liquid.

21.why: The digraph ѹ must be respelled because Milena deletes it — "ѹкъ" is byte-identical to "къ" (d2a5a27a) — and у is precisely what it is respelled as, in the recension as in every printed Slavonic book that uses the monograph. The vowel is stressed and alone, so it arrives as a full back [u] with no reduction, and the hard sign is mute: [uk].
21.compromise: Nothing is lost phonetically; the loss is graphic and worth telling the reader. Ѹ, оу and Ꙋ are three spellings of one letter, all still printed, and none of them is audible — the ear cannot tell you which sort the scribe drew. The name's own meaning is disputed, as the hall says, so there is nothing further the audio can settle.

22.why: 'Ферт' is a real Russian word — the letter name itself, preserved in the idiom 'стоять фертом' — so it is lexical, its stress is certain, and its vowel is full. The [f] is a clean labiodental fricative, which is the letter's whole business, since Slavic had no native f and this letter serves only loanwords and Greek names. Checked against the ё-trap by analogy with херъ; no competing ё-spelling exists.
22.compromise: The hall's headword is фрьтъ, with a jer between ф and р and no vowel before it; the recension form фертъ has resolved that into a full [e], so the audio gives a different syllable shape from the manuscript spelling. The final т is devoiced and the ъ mute. The name's etymology is, as the hall says, unexplained, and the audio has no opinion about it.

23.why: Russian х is a voiceless velar fricative [x] — the Scottish 'loch' sound the hall glosses — and no substitution is needed for the letter's own value. 'Хер' is a real Russian word (the letter name), so stress and vowel are lexical, and the mute ъ gives a clean monosyllable. Checked against the ё-trap: "херъ" and "хёръ" are different files (de30d809 against f2996539).
23.compromise: The ѣ of the headword хѣръ is respelled as е, which is the recension's own reading of that letter, so the vowel is [e] and specifically NOT the long lower vowel the reconstruction gives it. Before the front vowel Russian х is slightly fronted towards [xʲ], a shade more palatal than the plain velar the letter usually stands for; to hear the unfronted version, listen to the same fricative in the reconstruction's 'chéru', where Czech supplies it before a back vowel.

24.why: Milena deletes ѡ, so the name must be spelled with plain о — which is exactly right, because the recension does not distinguish this letter from о in speech at all, as the hall's own gloss says. 'Омега' is a real Russian word, so the stress is lexical and falls on the middle syllable where оме́га carries it. Checked against the ё-trap: "омега" and "омёга" are different files.
24.compromise: Akanye takes both unstressed vowels: the initial о reduces to [ɐ] and the final а to [ə], so you hear [ɐˈmʲeɡə] where a lector says [oˈmeɡa]. Two names for this letter are current in the Russian tradition, омега and отъ, and the second belongs properly to the Glagolitic letter and to the ligature Ѿ, as the hall explains; only the first is voiced here. The letter's own sound is in the audio, but it is in the first syllable and it is the reduced one.

25.why: This is the living name and the living value together. The Russian recension no longer reads щ as the OCS cluster [ʃt]; it reads it as modern Russian does, and Milena's щ is that sound — a long palatal fricative [ɕː], or [ɕtɕ] in more conservative usage. The vowel is stressed and full. Rate 140 as for every monosyllable here.
25.compromise: The letter's shape records a cluster the audio does not contain. Щ is ш drawn over т and it wrote [ʃt]; what you will hear has neither the [ʃ] nor the [t] in recoverable form, having gone through [ʃtʃ] to a single long [ɕː]. That drift is the single largest sound change separating the two systems in this hall, and the reconstruction's Czech 'šta' is the direct comparison — click them in succession. Which of [ɕː] and [ɕtɕ] Milena produces cannot be determined without hearing it; both are current in Russian, and the more conservative church reading is closer to the second.

26.why: The living name, spelt as printed Church Slavonic spells it. Russian ц is a plain voiceless [ts] affricate, hard in every position, which is the letter's value exactly; and because ц is always hard, the following vowel is automatically [ɨ] whether one writes и or ы. A clean monosyllable at 140.
26.compromise: The hall's transliteration is 'ci' with an [i]; the recension has backed that vowel to [ɨ], so the living name and the transliteration diverge. The name is opaque in any case, as the hall says, so there is no meaning for the vowel to distort.

27.why: 'Червь' is a real Russian word — 'worm', the same word the letter is named for, unchanged in a thousand years — so it is fully lexical: certain stress, full vowel, and the soft sign correctly palatalising the final в. The initial affricate is the letter's own value. Checked against the ё-trap: "червь" and "чёрвь" are different files (d0e44911 against 8f688408), so there is no risk of [tɕɵrvʲ].
27.compromise: Russian ч is [tɕ], an alveolo-palatal affricate that is always soft; the hall glosses the Slavonic letter as [tʃ], postalveolar. The difference is audible to a trained ear and is a genuine Russian development. The headword чрьвь has a jer where this has a full [e], so again the syllable shape is the recension's, not the manuscript's — the reconstruction's Czech 'črvi' restores the syllabic r.

28.why: The name is the letter's sound plus a vowel, so the sibilant carries everything, and Milena's ш is a voiceless sibilant delivered on a stressed full [a]. The simplest recipe in the hall.
28.compromise: Russian ш is retroflex [ʂ], with the tongue tip curled back, where the Slavonic letter was postalveolar [ʃ] — the difference is small but it is the entire content of this clip, so it should be said. The reconstruction uses Czech, whose š is a true [ʃ], and the pair is the cleanest minimal comparison in the hall: same vowel, same syllable, one voice retroflex and one not.

29.why: The name of the sign, read as the recension reads it: initial е is [je], the vowel is stressed and full, and the letter's own ъ at the end is mute — which is precisely the fact the name is being used to demonstrate. So the clip both names the sign and shows what it does, or rather does not do.
29.compromise: The letter's own sound is absent from its name, and that absence is correct rather than a failure: by the time the recension took shape the back jer had stopped being a vowel and become a mere orthographic mark, and the audio is evidence of it. To hear the jer still sounding as a vowel — the state of affairs in the tenth century, and the thing that dates a manuscript — use the reconstruction, where it is spelled out as [u].

30.why: Milena deletes ꙑ outright — "букꙑ" is byte-identical to "бук" — so the name is written with the simplified ы that printed Church Slavonic and Russian both use, and that letter delivers the sound the name is about: [ɨ], a high central unrounded vowel with no equivalent in most of Europe. The name ends on it, and it is the stressed syllable, so it arrives full.
30.compromise: The initial е reduces to [ɪ]; a lector says [jeˈrɨ]. Stress placement is the risk: 'еры' is a marginal word in modern Russian and both е́ры and еры́ are recorded, so Milena's choice cannot be verified by duration. The recipe is written on the assumption of final stress, which puts the accent on the letter's own vowel — if she takes the first syllable instead, the [ɨ] arrives unstressed and slightly centralised but still recognisably itself, so the clip is informative either way.

31.why: The mirror of index 29, and deliberately the same shape so the two form an audible pair: [jer] against [jerʲ]. Here the letter's own ь does its living job, palatalising the preceding р, so the clip demonstrates the sign's modern function in the act of naming it. Verified distinct from the hard-sign name: "еръ" and "ерь" are different files (8fe5a56d against f6ec0889), which is the proof that Milena honours the two signs differently.
31.compromise: As with еръ, the sign's original value — a very short front vowel — is not in the audio, because the recension no longer has it. What you hear instead is what it became: a diacritic on the consonant before it. The distinction between this and index 29 is carried entirely by the final consonant's palatalisation, which is subtle; listeners unused to Russian may not hear it at all on one pass.

32.why: 'Ять' is a real Russian word — the name of this very letter, familiar from the pre-reform orthography debates — so it is fully lexical. And it does something no respelling could arrange: Russian /a/ between two palatalised consonants is fronted and raised to [æ], so the name comes out [jætʲ], with exactly the low front vowel that the southern manuscripts' jat is reconstructed to have had. The letter is named with a version of its own sound, which is rare in this hall.
32.compromise: The length is missing. Jat was a LONG vowel and this is a short one; rate does stretch it (0.663 s at 175 against 1.062 s at 110, so the handle is real) but the living track is kept at the uniform monosyllable tempo of 140, because slowing this one name and nothing else would misrepresent a length the recension does not have — modern Russian and modern Slavonic reading alike have no phonemic vowel length at all. There is a deeper point: the recension does not actually read ѣ as [æ]. It reads it as plain [e], as every other entry in this track shows. So the letter's NAME here preserves a vowel quality the letter's own READING has lost — which is a true and rather beautiful fact about the tradition, and worth putting on the page.

33.why: The letter names itself and Russian reads it identically to Slavonic: the glide [j] followed by a full back [u], one syllable. There is no reduction to fear because the vowel bears the whole utterance. Rate 140 so the glide is not clipped.
33.compromise: Nothing is lost. The only remark worth making is the hall's own: Greek had no letter for this sound and therefore left no numeral, so this is one of the letters that counts for nothing in either script.

34.why: Milena deletes ꙗ (zero-length file), so the name must be written with я — which is not an arbitrary substitute but this letter's direct descendant, as the hall's note says. The value is unchanged in the descent: [ja], a glide plus a full stressed open vowel.
34.compromise: The hall is emphatic that substituting я for ꙗ in a Slavonic WORD is a real error and not a variant, and that is worth repeating here, because this recipe does exactly that on the audio side. It is defensible only because the sound is genuinely identical and Milena will not read the older sort at all; nobody should take the clip as licence to write я in a Slavonic text. The spelling and the sound have parted company, and only the sound is being reproduced.

35.why: Ѥ is deleted by Milena, and in any case it drops out of the later recensions entirely — so what is offered is the sound it wrote, produced by the plain letter е, which in Russian and in the recension alike is [je] word-initially. Verified: `say -v Milena "е"` is byte-identical to "йе" (0e0a9290), which proves the iotation is really there and is not a spelling artefact.
35.compromise: This letter does not exist in the living tradition. It fell out of use in the later recensions, and a Russian lector meeting it in an old manuscript would simply read it as е. So the honest description is that the clip gives the sound the letter used to write, using the letter that replaced it — and that in the recension, index 5 (Есть) and this entry begin with one and the same sound, which is exactly why the separate letter became unnecessary. The distinction the letter existed to make is not audible here because it is no longer made.

36.why: A two-word descriptive name, given in its Russian form, at 150 so the phrase stays intelligible — the same slowing the Greek hall uses for its unfamiliar archaic names. The stressed [a] of малый is full and the final ы is a clean [ɨ]. Note that the letter ѧ itself cannot appear in the text: Milena deletes it, and its recension reading is in any case plain я.
36.compromise: The letter's own sound is not in its name, and here that matters more than anywhere else in the hall — because in the Russian recension the little yus HAS no distinctive sound left. The nasality is entirely gone; ѧ is read exactly as я, [ja], and survives as a spelling convention only, as the hall says. So this clip names a letter whose value the living tradition has abolished. The nasal vowel it once wrote can be heard only in the reconstruction. The unstressed vowels of юсъ and the final syllable are reduced as usual.

37.why: Spelt большии and not большій because Milena DELETES і — "большій" is byte-identical to "большй" (75e3cc24) — which would have produced a mangled word. With double и the phrase parses normally at 1.377 s. The ь correctly palatalises the л, and the stressed о is full.
37.compromise: The most conjectural entry in this track, and it should be marked as such on the page. The great yus is not used in Russian recension books at all: it was dropped, and a modern Russian lector has no reading for it — the traditional value assigned when one is needed is simply [u]. So this is a name for a letter the living tradition does not use, spoken in the living tradition's phonetics. The double и at the end is a spelling compromise forced by the voice, not the printed form. And as at index 36, the letter's own nasal vowel is nowhere in the audio. Bulgarian kept this letter in its orthography until 1945 and Polish still writes the vowel as ą — the reconstruction reaches it through Polish.

38.why: The descriptive name in full, with йотованный spelt with й rather than the і- of іотованный, since Milena deletes і. Parses as three words at 1.910 s at this rate. The doubled нн gives a genuinely long [nː], which Russian has and which is correct for the participle.
38.compromise: A long descriptive label rather than a letter name proper, and the letter's own sound — the nasal [ɛ̃] preceded by j — appears nowhere in it. The word йотованный carries three reduced vowels, [jə.tɐˈva.nːɨj], where church reading would keep them full; at 150 words per minute the reduction is somewhat less severe than it would be at speed, but it is there. This letter has no place in the Russian recension, so what is being spoken is a philologist's label in a lector's accent.

39.why: Built exactly as index 38, with the same і-avoidance in both большии and йотованный, so that the two iotified yuses form a matched pair differing only in the middle word. Parses at 1.993 s.
39.compromise: Everything said at indices 37 and 38 applies at once, and this is the weakest entry in the living track. The rarest of the four yuses and the first to disappear, it has no recension reading whatever; the label is modern and descriptive; the double и is a spelling forced by the voice; and the letter's own [jɔ̃] is absent. What the clip honestly offers is a way of referring to the letter, not a way of pronouncing it.

40.why: Ѯ is deleted by Milena — "ѯи" comes out identical to "ѱи" (58d2542c), both reduced to the bare vowel — so the name is spelt out as кси, which is both the Russian name of the Greek letter and the letter's own value written in ordinary Cyrillic. Russian keeps initial [ks] fully, with no aspiration on the k, and reads it as a word at 0.708 s.
40.compromise: Russian palatalises the s before и, so what you hear is [ksʲi] rather than the plain [ksi] the letter stands for — a small softening of the second element of the cluster. The letter is purely Greek and was kept only for Greek words and numerals, so a lector encounters it rarely; the name is the Greek letter name and carries no Slavic sense at all.

41.why: Spelt out for the same reason as ksi and paired with it deliberately, since ѯ and ѱ are the matched stop-plus-sigma imports. Russian keeps word-initial [ps] fully pronounced — English structurally cannot, saying [saɪ] — and Russian [p] is unaspirated, which is correct for the cluster. Parses at 0.673 s.
41.compromise: The same palatalisation of the sibilant as at ksi: [psʲi] for [psi]. Like ksi this letter has no Glagolitic counterpart and no Slavic business; the audio is a Greek letter name read by a Russian voice, which is exactly what happens when a lector meets it.

42.why: Milena deletes ѳ — "ѳита" is byte-identical to "ита" (e8f71eee) — and ф is the respelling, which is exactly what the recension reads the letter as: [f], whatever its Greek origin, as the hall's own gloss says. 'Фита' is a real Russian word, the letter's name, stressed on the final syllable, so that vowel is full. Checked distinct from any ё-spelling.
42.compromise: The pretonic и reduces to [ɪ]; a lector says [fiˈta]. The interesting point is not a defect: the letter's Greek ancestor was θ, and the Slavonic tradition simply reassigned it to [f], so the name announces the sound the Slavs gave it rather than the sound the Greeks had. That reassignment is why Ѳеодоръ is Feodor and not Theodore in Russian. Nothing in this hall can produce the Greek [θ], and nothing should — it is not the Slavonic value.

43.why: Milena deletes ѵ, and 'ижица' is a real Russian word — the letter's own name, the last letter of the pre-reform alphabet and the one whose abolition in 1918 is still remembered — so it is lexical, with certain first-syllable stress and a full stressed [i]. Parses at 0.808 s.
43.compromise: The final а reduces to [ə], and the unstressed и after ж is retracted to [ɨ]; a lector says [ˈiʒitsa]. More important, the letter's own value is not in its name and could not be, because it has two: [i] in most positions and [v] after а or е, as in Паѵелъ. The name begins with the first of them, which is at least a partial demonstration. The etymology from иго, 'yoke', is traditional and the audio cannot bear on it.

ocs.note: The tenth-century canon as Slavists read it aloud: nasal vowels sounding, [dz] and [ʃt] intact, jers still vowels. Russian is almost useless here — it deletes nine of these letters and reduces every unstressed vowel — so the reconstruction is built on Polish, the only living language with the nasals, [ɨ], [dz] and [dʑ] and no vowel reduction, and on Czech, which supplies the postalveolar sibilants, phonemic vowel length and syllabic [r̩] that Polish lacks. Two letters are voiced elsewhere, each for a stated reason.

0.why: Polish gives a clean open [a] under stress with no reduction of any kind, a voiced [z] between vowels, and Polish stress on a disyllable is penultimate — that is, initial — which is where а́зъ carries it. The final u spells the back jer as a vowel, which is what a Slavist does when reading OCS aloud, and it also avoids Polish word-final devoicing: the bare form 'az' would end in [s].
0.compromise: The jer is too strong. Ъ wrote an ultra-short lax back vowel, and what you hear is a full, clearly articulated [u] — the right quality but roughly twice the right duration, so 'azъ' arrives as a solid two-syllable word where the manuscript had a syllable and a half. This is the standing compromise on every jer in this track. There is a real alternative and it is worth naming rather than hiding: Milena reading "азо" gives [ˈazə], because Russian post-tonic о reduces to a genuine schwa — the one place in this hall where akanye is an asset. It buys the right quantity by sacrificing the right quality, and it drags Russian phonetics into the word, so it is not used. The stress is Polish's, fixed; see the note on accent at index 4.

1.why: Polish y is [ɨ], the high central unrounded vowel that ꙑ writes, and Polish has it as a full unreduced phoneme in any position — this is one of the two things Polish is here for. The initial [b] is a true voiced stop, which is the letter's entire reason for existing: Byzantine beta had already become [v], so Cyrillic needed a new sort for [b] and gave it no numeral. Penultimate stress falls on бу, correctly. Parses as a word at 0.808 s.
1.compromise: Very little is lost. Polish [ɨ] is if anything slightly more retracted than the OCS vowel is usually reconstructed, and the final syllable, being unstressed in Polish, is a shade shorter than a full OCS vowel — but Polish does not reduce quality, so it stays [ɨ] rather than drifting to schwa. Compare with Milena's 'букы' in the living track, where the same vowel arrives with a Russian colour.

2.why: Two long vowels are wanted and Czech is the only voice on this machine that has phonemic vowel length — and it honours the acute that writes it, which was established by hashing: "vede" runs 0.544 s and "védé" 0.693 s, a 150 ms difference across two vowels, consistent and repeatable (the same +70 ms per acute appears at 'chéru' and 'jéty'). So the two jats come out genuinely long, [ɛː], not merely slow. Czech v is a clean [v]; Czech d before é is NOT palatalised, unlike before ě or i, so [dɛː] arrives plain; and Czech stress is fixed initial, matching вѣ́дѣ.
2.compromise: The quality is a compromise between the two regional jats and is squarely neither. The hall says jat was nearer [æ] in the south and [je] in the east; the OCS canon is southern, so [æː] is the target, and Czech é is [ɛː] — higher than [æ], lower than [e]. No installed voice can give a long [æː]: the only [æ] available anywhere in this hall is Russian's, at index 32, and it is short. So this is the right length with an approximate quality, and index 32 is the right quality with an approximate length; between the two clips the reader gets both halves of the vowel, which is the best this toolkit can do. This is also the letter whose name is most often cited in the later form вѣ́ди — that variant is the one voiced in the living track.

3.why: Polish gives a plain voiced velar stop [ɡ] twice — no fricativisation, no prenasalisation — a clear [l], a full unreduced [a], and [ɔ] for o, which is exactly the value the hall assigns to Slavonic о. Polish penultimate stress lands on -go-, which is where глаго́ли carries it: this is one of the few names where Polish's fixed accent happens to coincide with the tradition's. Note the spelling must be plain l, never ł, since Polish ł is [w].
3.compromise: Polish palatalises l before i, so the final syllable is [lʲi] rather than a plain [li] — a light Polish colouring on a syllable that is not the letter. Nothing else is lost; the letter's own value is delivered twice and cleanly, and it is worth telling the reader that this word is the source of the name Glagolitic, so the older script is called, in effect, 'the speaking'.

4.why: 'Dobro' is a real Polish word with the same meaning as the Slavonic — so it comes from Zosia's lexicon, not from letter-to-sound guessing — and it delivers what Russian cannot: BOTH o's as full unreduced [ɔ]. That is оканье, the rule Church Slavonic reading demands and Milena cannot obey. A true voiced [d] and a Polish alveolar trill complete it. Click this against the living track's 'добро' and the whole difference between the two systems is audible in one word.
4.compromise: The stress is Polish's — fixed penultimate, so initial on a disyllable — where the tradition says добро́, on the final syllable. That cannot be moved: Polish stress is not steerable by spelling or diacritic. It matters less than it looks, and this is the place to say why, because it applies across this whole track: OLD CHURCH SLAVONIC ACCENTUATION IS NOT DIRECTLY ATTESTED. The canonical manuscripts are unaccented, and every stress cited for these letter-names comes from the later Church Slavonic tradition, not from the tenth century. So Polish's fixed accent is not demonstrably wrong here; it is simply Polish's, and no claim is made for it. What is claimed is the vowels, and those are right.

5.why: Czech e is [ɛ], which is the hall's value for this letter, and Czech does not reduce it. The initial j is a clean glide, the [st] cluster is unaspirated, and the final u spells the back jer. Czech rather than Polish because Polish 'je-' is fine but Czech's [ɛ] is the more neutral mid vowel and Czech initial stress matches. Parses at 0.703 s.
5.compromise: As at index 0, the jer arrives as a full [u] where it was ultra-short. And the name given here is the hall's ѥстъ, spoken with the iotation the separate letter ѥ writes — but the letter at this index is plain Е, whose value is the bare vowel [ɛ] without the glide. So the first sound you hear is not, strictly, this letter's sound; it belongs to index 35. That is a property of the traditional name, not of the recipe, and the two clips together make the distinction audible.

6.why: Czech ž is a postalveolar [ʒ] — the 'measure' sound the hall glosses — where Polish ż is retroflex [ʐ] and Russian ж is retroflex and hard; Czech is the closest of the three to the palatal sibilant OCS had. Czech also keeps plain [i] after it, where both Polish and Russian would retract the vowel to [ɨ]. And the acute on é buys a genuinely long jat ("živete" 0.743 s against "živéte" 0.798 s, the same +55–70 ms the length mark produces elsewhere). No reduction anywhere.
6.compromise: Czech stress is fixed initial, so the word comes out [ˈʒivɛːtɛ] where the tradition says живѣ́те with the accent on the long jat — one of the places where Czech's fixed accent and the traditional stress disagree, and it cannot be moved. See index 4 on why that is a weaker objection than it appears. The jat is [ɛː] rather than [æː], as at index 2. Czech short i is slightly lax, [ɪ]-ward.

7.why: This is the letter Polish is indispensable for. Ѕ writes the affricate [dz] produced by the second and third palatalisations of g, and Polish has [dz] as a native, frequent phoneme spelt exactly 'dz' — no other installed language does. Czech's dz is marginal and loan-restricted; Russian has lost the sound entirely and the recension reads the letter as a plain [z]. Polish also gives [ɛ] and an unreduced final [ɔ], and penultimate stress on the first syllable, matching ѕѣ́ло. Parses at 0.713 s.
7.compromise: The jat is short [ɛ], not the long lower vowel of index 2 — Polish has no vowel length, and no voice on this machine has both [dz] and a long vowel, so this letter has to choose, and it chooses the affricate, since that is the letter's whole point. Note also that 'dz' could in principle be parsed as two segments rather than one affricate; Polish phonotactics make the affricate reading overwhelmingly likely word-initially, but this cannot be confirmed by duration. Compare the living track, where the sound is simply gone.

8.why: Czech gives a clean voiced [z], an unreduced [ɛ] where Russian would say [ɪ], and reads the 'lj' sequence as [lj], a good rendering of the palatal lateral the manuscripts write with л҄. The final a is full. Parses as one word at 0.758 s.
8.compromise: Stress is Czech's initial rather than the traditional final землꙗ́; see index 4. The [lj] is a lateral plus glide rather than a single palatal segment [ʎ] — audibly close, structurally not the same thing. Czech has no palatal lateral and neither does Polish, so this is the ceiling for this sound. The pretonic vowel is the point of comparison with the living track, where Russian ikanye reduces it to [ɪ].

9.why: Czech for the same reason as at index 6: ž is postalveolar [ʒ], not retroflex, and the final e stays a full [ɛ] where Russian would retract it to [ɨ] after the hushing consonant. Czech stress is initial, matching и́же. Parses at 0.673 s.
9.compromise: Czech short i is lax, [ɪ] rather than the tense [i] the letter stands for — a real if small mismatch on the letter's own vowel. Writing 'íže' would give a tense [iː] but at the cost of making it long, which it was not, so the laxness is accepted rather than traded for a false length. Polish would give a tense [i] but only with a retroflex ż after it; that trade was judged worse, since the vowel error is smaller than the sibilant error. This letter and index 10 are homophonous, then as now.

10.why: The letter names itself, and 'i' is a real Czech word (the conjunction 'and'), which is also this letter's meaning — so the token is lexical and is read as a word rather than as a letter name. Rate 140 as for every monosyllable in this track, so that a single light vowel is not clipped to nothing. Verified non-empty at 0.718 s.
10.compromise: Czech short i is lax [ɪ] rather than tense [i], as at index 9. Nothing distinguishes this clip from the vowel of и́же and nothing should: the two i-letters differ in shape, in numeral value and in scribal taste, never in sound. The Cyrillic character і itself must not be used in any text on this machine — Milena deletes it outright — but that constraint does not bite here, since Czech is doing the work.

11.why: Polish 'dzi' before a vowel is [d͡ʑ], the alveolo-palatal affricate the hall gives as this letter's value, and Polish is the only voice installed that has it — Russian has no [dʑ] at all and Czech's nearest sound is [ɟ] or [dʒ]. Polish also supplies a trilled r and, in the final i, a vowel for the front jer. Parses at 0.778 s. The same recipe serves both systems, since neither the Russian recension nor the OCS canon can supply an alternative.
11.compromise: The hall's gloss allows two readings — [dʑ] or the plain palatal stop [ɟ] — and this gives only the first; nothing here can produce [ɟ]. The final i is a full vowel where the jer was ultra-short, and Polish palatalises the preceding r to [rʲ], which is a Polish habit rather than a Slavonic fact. The deeper caveat is about the letter itself: it is marginal in the Cyrillic canon, at home in Glagolitic and in later Serbian usage, so its 'correct' OCS pronunciation is thinly attested and this recipe reproduces a value inferred largely from the Serbian ђ. Marked medium for the target, not the mechanism.

12.why: Polish rather than Czech specifically for the final vowel: Polish o is [ɔ], the open-mid back vowel the hall gives as Slavonic о, where Czech o is a closer [o]. Polish [k] is unaspirated, as Slavonic [k] was — an English voice would have aspirated both stops. Both vowels are full and unreduced, and penultimate stress falls on ка, matching ка́ко. Parses at 0.738 s.
12.compromise: Essentially nothing is lost; this is among the two or three most accurate recipes in the hall. The one thing worth pointing the reader at is the contrast with the living track, where the same word ends in a reduced schwa — како and кака are not distinguishable in Milena's mouth and are perfectly distinct here.

13.why: Czech is chosen here for the stress: this is a three-syllable name accented on the first in the tradition, лю́диѥ, and Czech's fixed initial stress delivers that where Polish's fixed penultimate stress would have put the accent on -di-. Czech also keeps all three vowels full and gives plain [i] rather than [ɨ]. The 'lj' renders the palatal л҄ the hall notes. Parses as one word at 0.748 s.
13.compromise: As at index 8, [lj] is a lateral plus a glide rather than a true palatal [ʎ]. The letter's OTHER value, the plain non-palatal [l], is not in the name at all — every occurrence of л here is the palatal variant. Czech short i is lax. The word is still the ordinary plural of 'person' across Slavic, unchanged, which is worth saying on the page.

14.why: Polish for the ꙑ: the first syllable must carry [ɨ] and only Polish has it as a full vowel — Czech y is simply [i], which would erase the ꙑ/и distinction that this name and буки both depend on. Polish also keeps the final e as a full [ɛ] and the medial i as [i], where Russian reduces both to [ɪ]. Parses at 0.923 s.
14.compromise: The stress is wrong and cannot be fixed: Polish's fixed penultimate accent puts it on -sli- where the tradition says мꙑ́слите, on the first syllable. This is the one name where Polish's stress rule and the traditional stress collide over the letter's own most distinctive vowel, so the [ɨ] arrives unstressed. It is still a full, unreduced [ɨ] — Polish does not reduce quality — but it is not prominent. Milena's 'мыслите' has the stress right and the other two vowels wrong; the segments were preferred. See index 4 on the standing of these traditional stresses.

15.why: Czech š is [ʃ], postalveolar, which is what the hall glosses — Polish sz and Russian ш are both retroflex and audibly further back. Czech also gives a full unreduced [a] and initial stress, matching на́шь, and the final i spells the front jer. Parses at 0.634 s.
15.compromise: Two things. The jer is a full [i] where it was ultra-short, as everywhere in this track. And the softness the ь writes lands on the vowel rather than the consonant: Czech š does not palatalise, so you hear [ʃɪ] rather than a palatalised [ʃʲ]. That said, the OCS sibilant was itself palatal, so the target is closer than the spelling suggests. As at index 13, the letter's palatal variant н҄ is not in the name.

16.why: Polish for the vowel: o is [ɔ], exactly the open-mid quality the hall assigns to this letter, where Czech would give a closer [o] and Russian a close-mid [o]. Penultimate stress falls on the letter's own vowel, correctly, and the final u spells the back jer. Parses at 0.629 s.
16.compromise: The jer again arrives as a full [u], and here it does a little more damage than elsewhere because the word is short and the two vowels end up near-equal in weight, where о́нъ should be one strong syllable and a fragment. The broad variant Ѻ ѻ, used at word-beginnings, is a graphic distinction only and has no separate sound to record.

17.why: One of the best recipes in the hall. 'Pokoi' is a real Polish word, so it is lexical; Polish initial [p] is unaspirated as Slavonic [p] was; BOTH o's are full open-mid [ɔ] with no reduction whatever; and Polish penultimate stress lands on -ko-, precisely where поко́и carries it. Every single feature the name needs arrives natively. Parses at 0.863 s.
17.compromise: Almost nothing. Polish inserts a light [j] glide between the o and the i, giving [ˈkɔji] rather than a clean hiatus — which is arguably right anyway, since the final -и of покои is generally read as a glide. Set this against the living track's 'покои', where the first vowel is reduced to [ɐ]: the pair is the single clearest demonstration of оканье in the hall, because here the two identical vowels really do sound identical.

18.why: Czech c is [ts] in every position, and Czech does not palatalise s or c before i the way Polish does — Polish 'ci' is [t͡ɕi], a quite different affricate, which rules Polish out here. The initial r is a Czech alveolar trill, the letter's own value. The i between r and c spells the front jer as a vowel. Parses normally at 0.614 s.
18.compromise: A genuinely instructive rejection sits behind this recipe and should be recorded. Czech HAS the exact word: 'rci' is the archaic imperative of říci, 'say!', the direct cognate of рьци and the same word in the same sense. It cannot be used. `say -v Zuzana "rci"` runs 1.063 s where comparable Czech monosyllables run 0.71–0.84 s ('ci' 0.728, 'si' 0.713, 'psi' 0.838) — the signature of a token being spelled out rather than read, and 'rcí' is worse still at 1.776 s. Slovak Laura fails identically (1.137 s against 0.454 s for 'ci'). Being a real word is no guarantee the synthesiser knows it. So the jer is written as a full vowel instead, which makes the word two clean syllables where OCS had a syllable and a fragment, and shifts the stress to the first. Whether the r surfaces as a full trill or a single tap cannot be established here.

19.why: Polish for the two o's: both come out as full open-mid [ɔ], which is the whole point, since this is the word that renders logos at the opening of John and the living track cannot say it without reducing the second vowel to schwa. Polish initial s before l is voiceless. Written 'slowo' and not 'słowo' because Polish ł is [w] — verified that the two spellings produce different audio (436013b8 against a7414309) at identical duration, which is exactly what substituting [l] for [w] should do. Penultimate stress on сло, matching сло́во.
19.compromise: The one uncertainty is the l. 'Słowo' is the real Polish word and 'slowo' is not, so the recipe depends on Zosia applying her letter-to-sound rule for bare l rather than normalising to the familiar word; the differing hashes say she does not normalise, but they cannot prove the segment is [l] rather than something else. If it were wrong the word would arrive as [ˈswɔvɔ]. Marked high rather than certain on that account. Click against the living track's 'слово' to hear оканье.

20.why: 'Tvrdo' is a real Czech word with a SYLLABIC [r̩] — Czech is the only voice installed that has syllabic liquids, and a syllabic r is the best available rendering of the Slavonic sequence -рь- before a consonant, where the jer had already become little more than a colouring on the liquid. So this reproduces the syllable structure of тврьдо rather than resolving it into a full vowel the way the Russian recension does with тве́рдо. Czech [t] is unaspirated, and Czech stress is initial as тврь́до requires. Parses at 0.693 s.
20.compromise: Two things. This treats the jer as absorbed into the liquid rather than as a separate vowel, which is a defensible reading of late OCS but not of the earliest canon, where ь before a liquid was probably still a distinct ultra-short vowel — so this recipe and the jer-as-vowel recipes elsewhere in the track are not applying one rule consistently, and the reason is that Czech offers something here it does not offer anywhere else. Second, Czech o is a close-mid [o] where the hall wants [ɔ]; Polish would have given the right vowel but has no syllabic r, and the syllabic r was judged the more distinctive feature. Compare the living track, where this letter's name has neither.

21.why: Polish u is a full back [u] in both stressed and unstressed position with no reduction, and Polish [k] is unaspirated. Penultimate stress falls on the letter's own vowel. The final u spells the back jer. Parses at 0.708 s.
21.compromise: This is the one name where the jer's full realisation as [u] does real harm, because it makes the word two identical vowels — [ˈuku] — where the letter's own [u] should be the long strong one and the jer a fragment. A listener may reasonably hear the second syllable as being the letter. Rate cannot separate them, since it scales the whole utterance. Nothing here bears on the disputed sense of the name, and nothing can: ѹ, оу and Ꙋ are three spellings of one sound.

22.why: Built exactly like 'tvrdo' at index 20, and for the same reason: Czech's syllabic [r̩] reproduces the -рь- of фрьтъ without inserting the full vowel that the later фертъ has. The [f] is a clean labiodental fricative, which is the letter's whole business — Slavic had no native f, so this letter serves only loanwords and Greek names. Czech [t] is unaspirated; the final u spells the back jer. Parses at 0.629 s.
22.compromise: The same inconsistency flagged at index 20: the jer before the liquid is absorbed while the word-final jer is spelled out as a vowel. Beyond that, the honest position is that nobody knows what this name means — the hall says no convincing Slavic etymology has been offered — so there is no sense for the audio to respect or betray. The syllabic-r reading assumes фрьтъ rather than фрътъ; the manuscripts vary and the choice is the hall's headword, not a finding.

23.why: Czech ch is a voiceless velar fricative [x] — the Scottish 'loch' sound the hall glosses — and here, unlike in the living track, it stands before a back-of-mid vowel and is not fronted, so it is the plain velar rather than a palatalised variant. The acute buys a genuinely long jat: "cheru" 0.584 s against "chéru" 0.644 s, the same 60 ms the length mark produces at 'védé' and 'jéty'. Czech stress is initial, matching хѣ́ръ. The final u spells the back jer.
23.compromise: The jat is [ɛː] rather than the southern canon's [æː], as at index 2 — the right length, an approximate quality. The jer arrives as a full [u]. The traditional derivation of the name from хероувимъ, 'cherub', is attractive and old but unproven, as the hall says, and the audio has no bearing on it either way.

24.why: 'Omega' is a real Polish word, so it is lexical, and Polish gives the initial o as a full open-mid [ɔ] — which is this letter's own value, and which the living track reduces to [ɐ]. Penultimate stress falls on -me-, where оме́га carries it, and the final a is full. Polish g is a plain voiced stop with no fricativisation. Parses at 0.758 s.
24.compromise: The letter's own sound is in the audio but it is the unstressed first vowel, so it is short — correct in quality, weak in prominence. More important is what the recipe cannot express: as the hall says, ѡ is not distinguished from о in speech at all, so this clip and index 16's 'onu' contain the same vowel, and no reading of any period would have distinguished them. The letter's whole life is graphic and numerical. Note too that the name отъ, 'from', belongs properly to the Glagolitic counterpart and to the ligature Ѿ, not to this letter, and is not voiced here.

25.why: The letter's shape is ш drawn over т and it wrote the cluster [ʃt]; Czech spells that cluster directly and reads it natively, with a postalveolar [ʃ] rather than the retroflex sibilant Polish and Russian would give. The vowel is a full [a]. Parses as a word at 0.828 s, in line with other Czech CCV monosyllables (compare 'psi' at 0.838 s), so there is no sign of it being spelled out. Rate 140 as for every monosyllable here.
25.compromise: Nothing is lost segmentally; this is one of the cleanest recipes in the hall. What should be said on the page is the comparison: the living track gives [ɕːa], a single long palatal fricative with no [t] in it at all, and the drift from this clip to that one — through [ʃtʃ] — is the largest single sound change separating the two systems. The hall's own gloss names both values. This is also one of the two letters with no Greek source at all, so its name is opaque and there is nothing for the audio to mean.

26.why: Czech c is [ts] in all positions and does not palatalise before i — where Polish 'ci' is [t͡ɕi], a quite different alveolo-palatal affricate, which rules Polish out for this letter as it did at index 18. So Czech gives [ts] plus a front vowel, which is the name exactly. Parses at 0.728 s, in line with 'si' (0.713) and 'ti' (0.713).
26.compromise: Czech short i is lax [ɪ] rather than tense [i]. Note a verified curiosity that bears on this track generally: `say -v Zuzana "ci"` and "cy" are BYTE-IDENTICAL (b991d0c4), which confirms that Czech y and i are one sound for this voice — which is why Czech can never be used where ꙑ must be distinguished from и, and why indices 1, 14 and 30 go to Polish. In the living track this letter's name has backed its vowel to [ɨ]; here it has not.

27.why: Czech č is [tʃ], postalveolar, which is the hall's gloss for this letter — where Russian ч is the alveolo-palatal [tɕ] and Polish cz is retroflex [tʂ], so Czech is the only one of the three that hits the target. And as at indices 20 and 22, Czech's syllabic [r̩] reproduces the -рь- of чрьвь without inserting a full vowel. The final i spells the second jer. Parses at 0.594 s.
27.compromise: The two jers are treated differently in one word — the first absorbed into the syllabic liquid, the second realised as a full [i] — which is the same inconsistency flagged at index 20 and is forced by what Czech can and cannot do. The word is 'worm', and the same root gives 'red', from the insect that yielded the dye; the audio cannot carry that, but the page can. Czech short i is lax.

28.why: The name is the letter's sound plus a vowel, so the sibilant is everything, and Czech š is a true postalveolar [ʃ] — the target — where Russian and Polish both give retroflex sibilants. A full unreduced [a] follows. Parses at 0.723 s.
28.compromise: Nothing is lost. This clip and the living track's 'ша' are the cleanest minimal pair the hall offers — identical syllable, identical vowel, and the only difference is that Milena's sibilant is retroflex and Zuzana's is not. The derivation of both the name and the shape from Hebrew shin is plausible and shared by both scripts, but remains an inference rather than a demonstration, and the audio has no bearing on it.

29.why: Czech gives a clean glide, a full [ɛ], a trilled r and no reduction; the final u is this letter's own sound, spelled out as the vowel it still was in the tenth century. So unlike the living track, where the name demonstrates the sign's silence, this clip demonstrates the sign's vowel — which is the whole difference between the two systems at this letter. Parses at 0.529 s.
29.compromise: The vowel is too strong, and here that is the substance of the entry rather than an aside. Ъ wrote an ultra-short lax back vowel — reconstructed [ŭ], with a quality somewhere between [u] and [ɤ] — and what you hear is a full, clear, ordinary [u]. Nothing installed can produce a genuinely reduced vowel of that kind on demand except Russian's post-tonic schwa, which has the wrong quality. So the clip is right about the fact that the jer was a vowel and wrong about how much of one. That the jer's weakening can be dated from manuscripts, and is one of the clearest ways of dating a copy, is precisely because it sat on this knife-edge — which the audio cannot show.

30.why: Polish, necessarily: the name ends in the letter's own sound and that sound is [ɨ], which only Polish has as a full unreduced vowel — Czech y is simply [i] and would erase the very distinction the letter exists to make. Polish also gives a full [ɛ] and a trilled r. Penultimate stress on the first syllable. Parses at 0.683 s.
30.compromise: Two things. The letter's vowel is unstressed here, so it is short, though Polish keeps its quality intact. And the stress placement is uncertain in the tradition itself — both е́ры and еры́ are recorded — so no claim is made about it. The hall's point that both scripts confess the same difficulty in the same way, Cyrillic by compounding jer with і and Glagolitic by writing a digraph, is worth putting beside the clip: the sound was hard to write, and it is audibly why.

31.why: The mirror of index 29, deliberately in the same voice and the same shape so the two form an audible pair — [ˈjɛru] against [ˈjɛrɪ] — which is exactly what ѥръ and ѥрь are to each other. The final i is the letter's own sound, the front jer, spelled out as the vowel it still was. Parses at 0.519 s, closely matching 'jeru' at 0.529 s.
31.compromise: The vowel is too strong, as at index 29: ь wrote an ultra-short front vowel and this is a full [ɪ]. Czech's short i is at least lax rather than tense, which makes it marginally the better of the two jers in this respect. The hall's warning about the names crossing between the scripts — Unicode calls the Glagolitic back jer YERU and the front jer YERI, while in Cyrillic 'yeru' is ы, a quite different letter — cannot be conveyed in audio at all, and this pair of clips is exactly the place a reader is most likely to get confused.

32.why: The one place Russian is the right tool in this track, and the reason is specific. Russian /a/ between two palatalised consonants is fronted and raised to [æ], so 'ять' — a real Russian word, the name of this very letter — comes out [jætʲ]: a low front vowel followed by a palatalised stop. That is the southern canon's jat, [æ], and NOTHING ELSE INSTALLED CAN MAKE IT. Czech and Polish both top out at [ɛ]; the Finnish and Danish voices have an [æ] but no Slavic consonant system to put it in. The rate is dropped to 130 (against 140 for other monosyllables) to lengthen the nucleus, since jat was long: verified that rate genuinely stretches this token — 0.663 s at 175, 0.863 s at 140, 1.062 s at 110 — so the handle is real, and 130 is chosen as the point where the vowel is audibly long without the consonants becoming grotesque.
32.compromise: Three honest points. (1) The length here is tempo, not phonemic quantity: the whole utterance is slowed, so the [tʲ] is stretched along with the vowel, which no reconstruction proposes. Czech could have given true phonemic length — that is how indices 2 and 23 get theirs — but only at [ɛː], the wrong quality. This letter chooses quality and buys length with the rate knob; those two clips choose length and accept [ɛː]. Between them the reader hears both halves of the vowel, and neither clip alone is the whole answer. (2) Akanye is not in play, because the vowel is stressed — this is the only word in the hall where Milena can be used safely. (3) The jat's quality genuinely varied by region from the very beginning: [æ] in the south, nearer [je] in the east, which is why the letters a scribe confuses it with tell you where he learned to write. A single clip cannot represent a sound whose whole interest is that it was not one sound.

33.why: The letter names itself: a glide plus a full back [u], one syllable, which Czech reads directly and without reduction. Rate 140 as for every monosyllable here, so the glide is not clipped. Parses at 0.673 s, matching 'ja' and 'je' exactly.
33.compromise: Nothing is lost. Czech u is slightly less rounded than a cardinal [u] but the difference is negligible. This is one of the iotified vowels for which Greek had no letters and therefore left no numerals, so the letter counts for nothing in Cyrillic — a fact the audio cannot carry.

34.why: 'Ja' is a real Czech word ('I') and is read as one: a glide plus a full open [a], with no reduction and no Russian orthographic substitution required — which matters, because the living track has to write this letter as я, its own descendant, and the hall is emphatic that doing so in a Slavonic word is an error rather than a variant. Here the sound is produced without the letter being misrepresented. Parses at 0.673 s.
34.compromise: Nothing is lost phonetically. Deliberately the same voice and rate as 'ju' and 'je' so the three iotified vowels form a set the ear can group, which is exactly what they are. The Glagolitic script has no separate letter here at all, pressing its jat into service for ja as well — a merger the audio cannot show, and one that later Cyrillic undid.

35.why: 'Je' is a real Czech word ('is'), which is also this letter's function in ѥстъ, so the token is lexical and the reading certain: a glide plus a full [ɛ], the hall's own value. Same voice and rate as indices 33 and 34. Parses at 0.673 s.
35.compromise: Nothing is lost. What should be said is what the letter is FOR: the plain vowel is written е and this separate sort writes it after j, a distinction Glagolitic does not make and the later recensions abandoned entirely. So the informative comparison is with index 5, whose traditional name ѥстъ actually begins with this sound rather than with its own — click the two and the distinction the letter exists to make is audible, which it is not in the living track, where the letter no longer exists.

36.why: Polish for the [ɨ] of малꙑи, which no other voice has, and Polish's total absence of vowel reduction keeps all four vowels full across a two-word phrase — which matters here, since Russian would have flattened три of them. Written 'maly' and not 'mały', since Polish ł is [w]. Rate 150 for the multi-word name, following the Greek hall's treatment of its unfamiliar archaic labels.
36.compromise: The letter's own sound is not in its name, and unlike index 37 there is no way to put it there. What can be done is to name the probe: Zosia reading "gęś" gives [ɡɛ̃ɕ], a real Polish word with the front nasal before a fricative, which is the position where Polish most reliably keeps the vowel genuinely nasal — that is the little yus's [ɛ̃], and it is the closest thing to a demonstration this toolkit affords. Polish's own nasals are also context-dependent: before a plosive they decompose into vowel plus nasal consonant, and word-finally ę is largely denasalised, so 'nasal vowel' is not something Polish can be relied on to produce just anywhere. The four-vowel name is otherwise clean. Compare the living track, where the nasality is not merely unheard but abolished — ѧ is read exactly as я.

37.why: Polish keeps every vowel full, gives [ɔ] in bol- (which is the correct Slavonic value), and supplies [ɨ] at the end. Written as a two-word phrase and parsed as one at 1.117 s. Rate 150 as at index 36 so the pair matches.
37.compromise: Two real losses and one thing worth knowing. Polish sz is retroflex [ʂ] where the Slavonic sibilant was postalveolar, and Polish l is plain, so the palatalisation the ь of большии writes is simply absent — you hear [bɔl-] where it should be [bɔlʲ-]. Neither can be fixed without giving up the [ɨ]. And as at index 36 the letter's own nasal vowel is absent from its name — but here there is a genuinely lovely probe, because the name itself is the sound. Юсъ descends from *ǫsъ, 'moustache', with the big yus in it; the modern Polish reflex of that very word is 'wąs', and Zosia reading "wąs" gives [vɔ̃s] — the letter's own vowel, in the letter's own name, in the one living language that kept it. That is the demonstration to put on the page.

38.why: Built on index 36 with the descriptive third word added, and Polish is the right voice for the whole phrase: 'jotowany' has four vowels, every one of which Russian would reduce and Polish keeps full — [jɔtɔˈvanɨ], with two clean [ɔ]s and a final [ɨ]. Parses as three words at 1.467 s.
38.compromise: A modern philologist's descriptive label rather than an attested tenth-century name, and it should be presented as such — no scribe called the letter this. The letter's own sound, [jɛ̃], is not in it; see index 36 for the probe. Polish sz-free here, so no sibilant problem, but the retroflex issue returns at index 39. Stress is Polish's throughout.

39.why: Built on index 37 exactly as index 38 is built on 36, so the two iotified yuses form a matched pair differing only in the middle word. All seven vowels arrive unreduced. Parses at 1.571 s.
39.compromise: Everything said at indices 37 and 38 applies together: the label is modern and descriptive, the retroflex sz is wrong for the Slavonic sibilant, the palatalisation of болььшии's l is lost, and the letter's own [jɔ̃] is absent from its name. This is the rarest of the four yuses and the first to go — often the letter a late copyist silently replaced when he no longer knew what it was for — so it is also the one for which the reconstruction is thinnest. The 'wąs' probe at index 37 gives the nasal vowel; nothing here gives it preceded by j.

40.why: The one non-Slavic voice in this track, and the justification is that this is not a Slavic letter: Ѯ is Greek ξ, kept in Cyrillic for Greek words and numerals, with no Glagolitic counterpart at all. German ⟨x⟩ is [ks] by native rule and 'Xi' is the German name of the letter, so the cluster is lexical, the k inside an initial cluster carries no aspiration, and German lengthens the stressed vowel in this open syllable. This is the identical recipe the Greek hall verified for Ξ — 0.549 s at default rate here, matching its 0.549 s exactly — so the same letter now sounds the same in both halls, which is right, because it is the same letter. Every Slavic option failed: Czech 'ksi' runs 1.053 s against 0.838 s for the comparable 'psi' and is not being read as a word (nor is Slovak's, at 1.167 s), and Polish 'ksi' is [kɕi], because Polish palatalises s before i.
40.compromise: The voice is German and the timbre changes audibly from everything around it. The vowel is long where the Slavonic name's и was short. Polish 'ksy' is the Slavic-voice fallback and reads normally at 0.574 s, but gives [ksɨ] — the right cluster on the wrong vowel — and was passed over for that reason. Note that this letter is purely ornamental in Slavic terms: it writes no native sound, and its presence, along with psi's, is one clear sign that Cyrillic was assembled by people working directly from Greek exemplars.

41.why: 'Psi' is a real Czech word ('dogs'), so it is lexical rather than guessed, and it reads normally at 0.838 s — in line with other Czech CCV monosyllables and unlike its partner ksi, which does not. Czech keeps word-initial [ps] fully pronounced where English structurally cannot (an English voice says [saɪ], dropping the p), and a stop at the head of an initial cluster is unaspirated, so the p is plain as ψ = π+σ requires.
41.compromise: The voice differs from its natural partner at index 40, which is a genuine inconsistency: ξ and ψ are the matched stop-plus-sigma imports and ought to sound like a pair. They do not, because the Czech token that works for psi does not work for ksi. Anyone who prefers the pair to match can use Anna 'Psi' — verified at 0.499 s and the Greek hall's own recipe — at the cost of a German voice on both. Czech short i is lax [ɪ] where the name's vowel was tense [i].

42.why: Czech gives a clean [f], full unreduced vowels, and an unaspirated [t]. Parses at 0.604 s. The name is spelled with f and not with any th-digraph deliberately: the hall's own gloss is that this letter is read [f] in Slavonic whatever its Greek origin, so a [θ] here would be importing Greek phonetics into a Slavonic reading — the specific error this track exists to avoid in the other direction.
42.compromise: Czech's fixed initial stress puts the accent on фи- where the tradition says фита́, on the final syllable; that cannot be moved. Czech short i is lax. The interesting caveat is about the target rather than the recipe: what OCS lectors actually did with Greek theta is not perfectly settled — Slavic borrowings show both т and ф as reflexes, and the [f] reading given here follows the hall and the later tradition rather than a demonstrated tenth-century fact. Marked medium on that account.

43.why: Czech reads this as a word at 0.843 s and gives everything it needs: ž as a postalveolar [ʒ] rather than the retroflex sibilant Polish or Russian would supply, c as a plain [ts], and three full unreduced vowels with initial stress, matching и́жица. Parses cleanly with no sign of spelling-out.
43.compromise: Czech short i is lax [ɪ] in both syllables where the name's vowels were tense [i]. More substantially, the letter's own value is not really in its name and could not be, because it has two — [i] in most positions, [v] after a preceding vowel, as in мѵро, the holy chrism, and Паѵелъ. The name begins with the first of them, which is a partial demonstration at best. The derivation from иго, 'the little yoke', is traditional and the audio has no bearing on it; nor can it show the more interesting fact that this letter, holding Greek upsilon's 400, is almost never actually put to numeral work in Slavonic, because ѹ already occupies that place.
